narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 68.9% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is well above the acceptance threshold, your law school application was rejected.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors from your academic record. Your class ranking at the end of your third year was the strongest influence and pushed the prediction strongly toward failure. Being in the bottom decile is far below the average of accepted students (around the middle of the class), signaling that your later-year performance raised serious concerns about readiness for the bar.

Your first-year class ranking was the next most important factor and also pulled the outcome toward failure. Again, a bottom-decile placement is much weaker than the typical accepted student, who sits near the sixth decile.

Your LSAT score worked in the opposite direction. At 37, it is almost exactly average for accepted students and therefore helped push the prediction slightly toward passing. Unfortunately, this positive signal was not large enough to overcome the two substantial academic-ranking concerns.

The model did not consider your gender or race in any way.

To improve your chances, you should focus on strengthening your academic trajectory. Retaking key courses, seeking targeted tutoring, or gaining additional legal experience that demonstrates growth could help show admissions committees that your early rankings do not reflect your full potential. Consider reapplying once you have clear evidence of improvement.
